prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Here lies, whom hound did ne’er pursue, Nor swifter greyhound follow, Whose foot ne’er tainted morning dew, Nor ear heard huntsman’s hallo’, Old Tiney, surliest of his kind, Who, nursed with tender care, And to domesticate bounds confined, Was still a wild jack-hare. Though duly from my hand he took His pittance every night, He did it with a jealous look, And, when he could, would bite. His diet was of wheaten bread, And milk, and oats, and straw, Thistles, or lettuces instead, With sand to scour his maw. On twigs of hawthorn he regaled, On pippins’ russet peel; And, when his juicy salads failed, Sliced carrot pleased him well. A Turkey carpet was his lawn, Whereon he loved to bound, To skip and gambol like a fawn, And swing his rump around. His frisking was at evening hours, For then he lost his fear; But most before approaching showers, Or when a storm drew near. Eight years and five round-rolling moons He thus saw steal away, Dozing out all his idle noons, And every night at play. I kept him for his humor’s sake, For he would oft beguile My heart of thoughts that made it ache, And force me to a smile. But now, beneath this walnut-shade He finds his long, last home, And waits in snug concealment laid, Till gentler Puss shall come. He, still more agèd, feels the shocks From which no care can save, And, partner once of Tiney’s box, Must soon partake his grave.

outputs.L1:
# Epitaph on a Hare

Here lies one whom hound did never pursue,
Nor swifter greyhound chase,
Whose foot ne'er brushed the morning dew,
Nor heard the huntsman's hallo'.

Old Tiney, surliest of his kind,
Who, nursed with tender care,
And though to gentle bounds confined,
Remained a wild jack-hare.

Though duly from my hand he took
His portion every night,
He took it with a jealous look,
And, when he could, would bite.

His fare was wheaten bread entire,
With milk, and oats, and straw,
Thistles or lettuce, to his desire,
With sand to ease his maw.

On sprigs of hawthorn he would dine,
On russet pippins' peel;
And when his succulent greens declined,
Sliced carrot pleased him well.

A Turkey carpet was his lawn,
Whereon he loved to bound,
To skip and gambol like a fawn,
And whirl his rump around.

His frolics came at evening's hour,
When fear no longer stayed;
But most before the threatening shower,
Or storm not far delayed.

Eight years, and five moons' waning light,
He thus saw glide away,
In idle dozing spent his days,
And every evening played.

I kept him for his humor's sake,
For he would oft beguile
My heart of thoughts that made it ache,
And win from me a smile.

But now, beneath this walnut shade,
He finds his last repose,
And waits, in quiet stillness laid,
Till gentler Puss shall close.

He too, more aged, feels the weight
From which no care can save,
And, once the partner of his state,
Must soon partake his grave.

---

*Note: This is a lightly refined rendering of William Cowper's well-known "Epitaph on a Hare," preserving the original content, structure, and sentiment while smoothing certain phrasings for enhanced clarity and flow. The poem commemorates Cowper's pet hare, Tiney, and reflects on mortality, companionship, and the quiet dignity of a domesticated wild creature.*
outputs.L2:
Here rests one whom no hound ever chased,
Nor swift greyhound gave pursuit,
Whose paws never touched the morning grass,
Nor ears caught the hunter's shout.
Old Tiney, most stubborn of his breed,
Who, raised with gentle attention,
And kept within tame boundaries,
Remained a wild hare in temperament.

Though he regularly accepted from my hand
His small ration each evening,
He accepted it with a suspicious glance,
And would bite whenever he had the chance.
His meals consisted of wheat bread,
Milk, oats, and straw,
Thistles or lettuce as alternatives,
With sand to help his digestion.

He enjoyed hawthorn twigs,
And the reddish-brown peel of apples;
When his green vegetables ran out,
He was content with sliced carrots.

A Turkish rug served as his meadow,
Where he loved to leap about,
Hopping and playing like a young deer,
Twisting his hindquarters as he moved.

His playful energy came alive in the evening,
When his timidity would vanish;
But especially before rain approached,
Or when a storm was gathering.

Eight years and five additional months
Passed by in this manner,
Sleeping through his lazy afternoons,
And playing every single night.

I kept him because his personality amused me,
For he often lifted
My troubled thoughts away,
And brought a smile to my face despite myself.

But now, under this walnut tree's shadow,
He has found his final resting place,
Waiting quietly hidden away,
Until the more docile Puss arrives to join him.

Puss, being even older, experiences the same afflictions
That no amount of caution can prevent,
And having once shared Tiney's enclosure,
Will soon share his burial place as well.
outputs.L3:
# Old Tiney: A Remembrance

Old Tiney was, in every essential respect, a creature of the wild—a jack-hare whose spirit refused to be tamed by circumstance, however gentle. Though he lived for years under careful domestication, receiving food, shelter, and attention that any wild creature would never know, he remained fundamentally himself: surly, suspicious, and ever alert to some imagined threat. He never learned to trust the hand that fed him, and indeed, when the mood struck him, he would bite—a small but persistent reminder that beneath his docile appearance lurked an animal who had never truly forgotten what he was. This wariness, this refusal to be softened by kindness, seemed almost a point of pride with him, as though he considered it beneath his dignity to surrender entirely to captivity.

Despite his prickly temperament, Tiney was tended to with remarkable care and attentiveness. His diet was varied and thoughtfully assembled: wheaten bread and milk formed a staple, supplemented by oats and straw for roughage, while thistles and lettuces provided the greens his nature craved. Hawthorn twigs offered him something to gnaw upon, apple peel added a touch of sweetness to his fare, and carrots rounded out this careful provisioning. Such attention to the particulars of his sustenance reveals not mere obligation but genuine devotion—a determination that whatever else Tiney might lack in affection toward his keeper, he would want for nothing in his care.

Yet for all his wildness, Tiney was not without his moments of unguarded joy. Upon the Turkey carpet that graced the room, he would frolic and gambol with an abandon that seemed to belie his otherwise guarded nature. These displays came most often in the evenings, when the day's business had quieted, and curiously, before storms—as though some instinct stirred in him at the change in the air, calling forth a burst of energy and movement. In these moments, something of his true, unguarded self seemed to emerge: a creature capable of play, of freedom, of pure animal delight, even if such moments were fleeting and never quite erased the wariness that defined him the rest of the time.

For eight years and five months, Tiney remained a companion—if such a word can be applied to so independent a spirit. Through this considerable span of time, his presence offered something valuable beyond mere company: a diversion from melancholy thoughts, a living creature whose antics and needs demanded attention and thereby drew the mind away from sorrow. There is a particular gift in the companionship of animals who ask nothing of our emotional investment yet somehow ease our burdens simply by requiring our care and occasionally rewarding us with moments of unexpected charm.

Now Tiney is gone. He lies buried beneath a walnut tree, a fitting resting place for a creature so tied to the natural world despite his years indoors. And in a quiet, almost inevitable turn, another hare—Puss, now himself advanced in age—continues on, though not for much longer. Puss will, in time, join Tiney beneath that same tree, or one like it, completing a cycle that speaks to the fleeting nature of even our longest-kept companions. There is something both sorrowful and fitting in this: that the creatures who accompany us through years of our lives, who never quite belong to us despite our care, must eventually return to the earth from which their wildness first came.

# An Epitaph for Tiney

Here lies Tiney, once a creature of the wild fields and hedgerows, who in the fullness of time came to dwell within the walls of a quiet household, fed by gentle hands and sheltered from every storm. For eight long years he lived among us, growing neither soft in spirit nor forgetful of the blood that ran in his veins from ancestors who knew only the open warren and the chase.

Though he wanted for nothing—his hutch was warm, his dish was full, his corner of the garden safe from hound and hawk—Tiney never surrendered the wildness that was his birthright. He remained, to the end, jealous of his space, quick to nip at the hand that lingered too long in affection, suspicious of intrusion even from those who loved him best. No amount of tenderness could tame what nature had made untamable; he was a wild thing still, however domesticated his circumstances.

And yet, for all his prickly independence, Tiney gave more than he received. In the quiet hours when the poet's heart grew heavy with sorrow, when the world seemed too full of grief and disappointment, it was often Tiney's small presence—his twitching nose, his watchful eye, his stubborn refusal to be anything other than himself—that offered a strange and simple comfort. There is something in the company of a creature who asks for nothing but tolerance that can ease even the deepest melancholy. In this way, Tiney was no mere pet but a companion of the spirit, easing burdens he could never have understood.

Now he is gone, laid to rest after those eight years of half-wild, half-sheltered life. His death comes as it must come to all living things, wild or tame, and it serves as a quiet, insistent reminder that no comfort of hearth or home can hold back the hand of time. Even creatures who seem to have found a peaceful accommodation with the world are not exempt from its final claim.

And here, beneath the same walnut tree that shaded Tiney's days, waits an empty space—for Puss, his fellow hare, grows old now too, and cannot be far behind. Soon enough she will join him in this quiet plot of earth, and the tree that once gave them both shade in life will stand sentinel over them both in death. So the poem stands not only as a tribute to one small creature's stubborn, untamed spirit, but as a meditation on mortality itself—on how even the gentlest care cannot stay the passing of all things, wild or gentled, into the ground beneath the walnut tree.
outputs.L5:
# Here, Nor, Whose

Here, in this quiet corner of the world, time seems to move differently. The old house stands as it has for generations, its walls holding stories that no one living can fully recall. Here is where my grandmother once tended her garden, where the scent of lavender still lingers faintly on summer evenings.

Nor does the passage of years erase what matters most. Nor can any distance—however vast—truly separate us from the places that shaped who we are. The roots we put down, whether in soil or memory, tend to hold fast against the pull of time and circumstance.

Whose hands first planted the oak tree in the yard, no one quite remembers. Whose voice echoes in the creak of the floorboards upstairs remains a mystery wrapped in nostalgia. Yet these unknowns don't diminish the significance of the space—if anything, they deepen it, adding layers of meaning to something already rich with history.

Here we return, again and again, drawn by an invisible thread. Nor should we resist that pull, for it connects us to something larger than ourselves—a continuity of experience, of belonging, of home. And whose story isn't, in some way, a reflection of the places they've loved and the people who came before them?

In the end, perhaps that's what "here" truly means: not just a location, but a convergence of memory, presence, and quiet reverence for whose lives intertwined with our own.

# An Epitaph for a Pet Hare

Beneath this turf, in slumber deep,
Where clover nods and daisies peep,
Lies one who knew nor guile nor strife,
A gentle hare that graced our life.

No hound's alarm, no huntsman's horn,
E'er stirred the peace in which she's born;
Within our hearth she found her home,
Nor ever wished the fields to roam.

Her eyes, like dew on morning grass,
Would watch the household figures pass;
Her velvet ears, so soft, so mild,
Bespoke a nature meek and wild.

She nibbled herbs with dainty care,
And thumped her joy upon the stair;
No lapdog's fawning, no bird's song,
Could to our hearts so sweet belong.

Now still those feet that loved to bound,
Now cold that heart with love so crowned;
Yet here, dear Fleet, thy gentle ghost
Shall guard the garden thou lov'st most.

Sleep on, sweet hare, beneath the yew,
Till fields of heaven bloom anew;
And may thy master, when he dies,
Find thee once more in Paradise.

---

**An Epitaph for Tiney, a Tame Jackrabbit**

Here lieth Tiney, jackrabbit tame and mild,
Who romped upon this lawn in days of yore,
A gentle creature, neither tame nor wild,
Who came unbidden to our cottage door.

No leash did bind him, yet he ne'er did stray,
Content to nibble clover in the sun,
He watched the children at their evening play,
And when the supper-bell rang, he would run

Unto the kitchen door to claim his share
Of crusts and carrots, offered with delight,
He was, in truth, no ordinary hare,
But friend and fixture of our household bright.

He feared no fox, for none did dare intrude
Upon a beast so cherished and so free;
He asked but clover, kindness, and his food,
And gave in turn his gentle company.

Now doth he lie beneath this garden green,
His final leap now leaped, his spirit fled,
The gentlest hare that ever here was seen—
Sweet Tiney rests among the peaceful dead.

*Reader, should you chance to pass this stone,
Spare one soft thought for creatures small and true;
Not every heart deserving is our own—
This humble hare had gentleness for two.*

**An Elegy Upon the Death of a Tame Hare**

*(in the manner of the last age)*

No more with soft and stealing pace
She seeks her wonted lawn,
Nor lifts her mild and startled face
To greet the breaking dawn.

Full nine long years beneath my roof
She dwelt in gentle ease,
And learned to know the friendly foot
That brought her bread and pease.

Her food was of the tenderest kind,
Green sorrel, mallow, mint,
The sweetest herbs that man could find,
And oats without a stint.

At morn she took her sop of bread
Soaked soft in new-drawn milk,
At eve on lettuce-leaves she fed,
Or cooling cress like silk.

She loved the twilight hour to roam
Across the parlour floor,
And thump her foot, as if the room
Were meadow, field, and moor.

No hound she knew, no horn, no chase,
Yet Nature's ancient fright
Would cross at times her gentle face
And send her swift from sight.

Beneath the stool, behind the chair,
She'd crouch with ears laid low,
Then venture forth, as if aware
No harm should man bestow.

Nine winters mild she passed within,
Nine summers in the shade,
Till age's slow and silent sin
Upon her frame was laid.

One autumn morn I found her laid
Upon her bed of hay,
As if in gentle sleep delayed,
Her spirit stole away.

No pang she knew, no cry, no strife,
But as a candle spent,
So calmly closed her harmless life,
So still to darkness went.

I laid her 'neath the garden tree
Where oft in life she played,
And there she sleeps eternally
Beneath the willow's shade.

Farewell, poor Puss, my gentle friend,
Companion of my days,
Thy little life has found its end,
But not without my praise.
